newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Tennis-Tearful Capriati overcome by cheers of crowd.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Tennis-Tearful Capriati overcome by cheers of crowd.

text.p: Former U.S. child star Jennifer Capriati burst into tears on Tuesday after tumbling out of the Australian Open, overcome by past torments and public support for her comeback.
A sobbing Capriati was escorted from a news conference after losing 6-2 3-6 6-4 to fellow American Jolene Watanabe and revealing that she wanted a new coach to replace her father.
A gold medallist at the 1992 Olympics, Capriati was playing in only her third grand slam tournament in four years after rebelling against the training regime of her childhood.
In more than two years off the circuit, she faced charges of drug possession and shoplifting.
When asked on Tuesday if she had sensed the public's warmth for her comeback, she started to reply "just being out there and hearing the cries..." before bursting into tears.
The New York-born player cried uncontrollably with her head in her hands for a number of seconds before tennis officials escorted her from the media room.
Capriati, ranked 24 in the world, is coached by her father Stefano, but revealed she was now looking for someone else.
"It's such a mental game, so I think one of the most important things is to find a coach right now," she said.
"But I'm not going to let this discourage me, let this get me down...I'll just just try to think positive still and go for the next one," Capriati said.
Watanabe, 28, said she felt for Capriati, who she said needed a friend more than anything else.
"I think she needs somebody else," said the 78th-ranked Watanabe, who rated the win as one of her best ever.
"It's difficult to have your father, have him as a father and a coach, it just gets too personal.
"She might need another coach just to be a friend too."
Playing in front of a packed crowd on an outside court, Capriati failed to come to terms with the windy conditions constantly spraying her shots long and wide.
But the crowd desperately cheered her on, hoping the former world number six could regain the form which carried her to final of the Sydney International last Saturday.
Capriati, a quarter-finalist in Melbourne at the age of 15 in 1992 and again the following year, missed the previous three Australian Opens.
